description: Question: when the wind doubles, why does a wind farm make far more than twice the power, and why can it never take all of it? Data: two months (September and October 2026) of metered half-hourly output of Westermost Rough, an offshore wind farm 8 km off Holderness, England (35 Siemens SWT-6.0-154 turbines, 6 MW each, 154 m rotors, 210 MW), from Elexon's BMRS (dataset B1610, BM unit T_WTMSO-1, free to use under the BMRS data licence with attribution); and hourly ERA5 reanalysis wind at 100 m, temperature and surface pressure at the nearest grid point from Open-Meteo's historical weather API (CC BY 4.0). Idea: the kinetic energy flux through a rotor is P = ½ ρ A v³: the mass of air per second (ρAv) times its kinetic energy per kilogram (v²/2). Doubling the wind gives eight times the power. A rotor can only take part of it: to extract energy it must slow the air, and stopping it would block the flow. Betz (1920) showed with momentum theory that the most a rotor can capture is 16/27 ≈ 59.3% of the power in the wind, when it slows the air to a third downstream. Steps: Elexon's half-hours to hourly MW; ERA5 to wind and air density; each hour with the power in the wind through the 35 rotors and the power coefficient Cp; the measured power curve in 0.5 m/s bins with the Betz limit; a log-log fit of output on wind below rated power (the exponent of the cube law); the energy share by wind speed; the two months in numbers. The aha: below rated power the farm's output goes as v^3.17 (611 hours from 4.5 to 10 m/s, r = 0.78): doubling the wind gives nine times the power and the bin medians stay well below the Betz line (median Cp 0.37 at 7–9 m/s against 0.593; the 84 single hours above it are where the 30 km ERA5 wind underestimates the wind at the farm); the windy hours carry the energy, because the mean of v³ is much larger than the cube of the mean v (the power in the wind averaged 510 MW, while the mean wind of 9.4 m/s cubed gives only 336 MW). The farm ran at a capacity factor of 54% and at its cap 17% of the hours. Above about 12 m/s the turbines cap their output on purpose (pitch control), so the cube law gives way to the rated plateau. Caveats: ERA5 wind is a 30 km grid value at 100 m, not the turbines' own anemometers, so the scatter is mostly measurement, and Cp mixes in wake losses inside the farm; curtailment (the grid operator paying the farm to stop) shows as hours of low output in high wind; output is net metered at the grid; the settlement run (II, SF, R1) can revise values. Next: look up the farm's curtailment (Elexon BOALF bid-offer acceptances for T_WTMSO-1) to explain the outliers, or compare a farm with larger rotors (Burbo Bank Extension, T_BRBEO-1, 8 MW turbines).
name: Wind power: the cube law and the Betz limit
